title: The overview effect
hookLine: astronauts often report a shift in how they see borders and the planet (Frank White, 1987)

cards: On Christmas Eve, 1968, three astronauts in Apollo 8 were circling the moon, busy photographing its gray, cratered surface for future landing sites.
Then, as they came around, Bill Anders saw something rising over the moon's edge: a blue and white half-ball, bright against the black. He snapped a black-and-white frame, then called for color film.
The color picture he took is called Earthrise. The crew had flown all that way to study the moon, and the picture people remember is of home.

teach.b: In 1987 a writer named Frank White published a book gathering what astronauts said about seeing Earth from space. He called the experience the overview effect. Again and again, the people he interviewed described a shift.
From orbit they saw a whole planet, glowing and thin-skinned, the atmosphere like a layer of varnish. Weather crossing continents, rivers running past countries, the night side lit by cities.

teach.h: THE LINES ON THE MAP AREN'T THERE.
teach.b: And they didn't see the lines on the map; most borders simply aren't there from above. Some said it changed how they thought about nations, about conflict, about the planet as one fragile home.
Edgar Mitchell, of Apollo 14, described a sudden, overwhelming sense of connection on the trip back from the moon, which changed the direction of his life.
To be honest about it: not every astronaut reports this, and those who do describe it in their own ways, some in religious terms, some in scientific ones, some in both.
Researchers have since studied it as a kind of awe, the feeling of standing before something so vast it rearranges your sense of yourself.
One more honest note: a few borders do show from space at night, like the lit fence between India and Pakistan. People built that light. The planet didn't.
That's the point several astronauts make: the lines are ours, and from up there, what shows is one world. Most of us will never go. But the night sky is a small, free version, and it's right outside.

how: Astronauts of many nations and faiths have described the overview effect, and some people on the ground seek a small version of it by looking at Earthrise, the Pale Blue Dot, or the night sky.

games.why: Bill Anders took a black-and-white shot, then called for color film. the color frame is Earthrise.

practice: Look up, outside or at a window if it's night, or in your mind if it's day, and find one star, or the moon, or just the dark.
Remember that you're standing on a turning planet with nothing underneath it but space, and everyone you know is standing on it too. Let yourself feel the size of it for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Earthrise. The photo Bill Anders took of Earth rising over the moon, and the shift astronauts often feel seeing the whole planet with no lines on it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: no borders from up there. A line between us and them may feel thick, but from orbit you can't see it. Day one hundred twenty-four.
